title: Perf Canary Phase 1 Retro Notes (us-east) — Initial Rollout
content:
Doc purpose
- Capture learnings from Phase 1 production rollout of the perf regression canary in us-east.
- Focus: what worked, what was noisy / surprising, and concrete actions for Phase 2 (expand models + regions, integrate rollout gates).

Rollout snapshot (Phase 1)
- Region: us-east
- Initial model coverage: 3 models (2 “top” + 1 “high-risk/new-kernel”) — kept intentionally small for tuning
- Canary traffic: synthetic prompt distribution (seeded) with prefill/decode mix + length buckets
- Alerts enabled:
  - Week 1: warning only
  - Week 2: paging enabled for top-model sustained regressions (after tuning)
- Primary signals monitored:
  - p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency
  - runtime-only latency (where available)
  - tokens/sec
  - prefill latency + decode latency
  - scheduler queueing time
  - batch size distribution

What worked well
1) Canary caught a real regression before wider impact
- We saw a sustained p95 regression on a top model shortly after a runtime rollout to a small slice.
- Canary alert + dashboard panels were enough to justify halting expansion while we investigated.
- The regression was real (not noise): it matched a subset of customer-facing perf complaints in internal monitoring but was detected earlier by the canary.
- Net: validated the core thesis that a lightweight always-on synthetic canary can catch tail regressions pre-broad customer impact.

2) Attribution signals materially improved time-to-triage
- Queueing time metrics were the biggest win for “is this scheduler/fleet vs runtime execution?”
  - When queueing time spiked, we could immediately shift focus to batching / capacity / noisy neighbor / fleet changes.
  - When queueing was flat but runtime-only latency rose, investigation went to kernels / runtime build.
- Kernel/runtime build tags being present on the dashboards avoided the “what changed?” Slack archaeology.
- Batch size distribution panel helped explain tokens/sec drops that were actually batching depth changes vs pure kernel regressions.

3) Incident-bot formatting + deep links reduced coordination overhead
- The alert payload linking directly to the per-model dashboard and the runbook reduced time spent asking “where do I click?”.
- Thread dedupe mostly worked (see noise section for remaining issues), but the overall UX was significantly better than our typical ad-hoc perf investigation flow.

4) Overhead budget stayed within bounds (with QPS caps)
- With the current caps + model coverage, estimated GPU overhead in us-east stayed under our target envelope.
- We did not see any inference endpoint saturation attributable to canary load.
- The explicit “disable switch” drill was successful; SRE was comfortable we can turn it off quickly if needed.

What was noisy / painful
1) Baseline drift + “slow change” created false positives
- We observed gradual shifts in baseline due to:
  - fleet composition drift (GPU SKU mix)
  - runtime scheduling tweaks that change batching patterns without being “regressions”
  - regional variability across the day (traffic mix / co-tenancy effects)
- Our initial baseline strategy was too sensitive to small but persistent shifts, which led to multiple warning-level alerts that were not actionable.
- Outcome: loss of confidence early in Week 1; required manual threshold bumping and dampening adjustments.

2) Cardinality pressure showed up sooner than expected
- Even with guardrails, label combinations (model x version x region x sku x runtime build x kernel id) can blow up quickly.
- We had to trim dimensions in a few places and re-aggregate to keep queries snappy and retention costs reasonable.
- Lesson: we need stricter “allowed label set” guidance and automated checks (pre-merge) rather than relying on reviewer vigilance.

3) Telemetry pipeline latency caused confusing alert timing
- In at least two cases, the dashboard lagged behind the alert by enough minutes to make on-call question the alert validity.
- This also complicated “minimum sample size” logic: samples existed at the canary service, but were not yet visible in the downstream query.
- We need to treat telemetry ingestion latency as a first-class dependency and expose it in the canary dashboards/alerts (or adjust evaluation windows).

4) Paging hygiene issues during the alert storm incident
- During the false positive alert storm:
  - dedupe keys were not stable across minor dimension changes
  - multiple alerts for the same underlying shift were treated as distinct
  - warning alerts sometimes fired “alongside” paging alerts, creating thread clutter
- Net: increased on-call load and reduced trust.

5) Synthetic prompt “shape” gaps (representation)
- The current prompt distribution covers common length buckets, but we likely under-sample:
  - very long context prefill paths (rare but painful for tails)
  - short prompt / long decode “chatty” workloads
  - KV cache hit/miss transitions (we don’t currently force cache reuse patterns consistently)
- Not a blocker for Phase 1, but important if we want high confidence for top models.

Decisions / changes already made (post-Phase 1, in-progress)
- Increased minimum sample sizes for paging alerts on top models; tightened evaluation window alignment with ingestion lag.
- Added additional dampening for warning-level alerts (reduce flapping).
- Trimmed/standardized metric labels and removed one high-cardinality tag from default emission.
- Updated runbook with a clearer decision tree: “queueing vs runtime-only” first.

Action items (Phase 2)
Priority P0 (must do before expanding paging to more models)
1) Baseline strategy update: drift-aware baselines
- Proposal: baseline per (model, model_version, sku) with controlled update policy
  - “fixed” baseline per runtime version during rollout windows
  - “rolling” baseline only when no active rollouts and drift is within guardrails
- Add explicit “baseline validity” signal (staleness, sample count, last refresh)
- Owner: Nadia Rahman
- Tracking: Linear ENG-4874 + ENG-4882
- Target: end of next sprint

2) Alert dedupe + severity unification
- Make dedupe key stable (model + region + sku + metric) and keep build/kernel metadata as annotations, not part of key.
- Ensure warning and paging alerts collapse into one Slack thread per key, with severity updates.
- Owner: Rafael Mendes (incident-bot) + Allison Grant (alerting standards)
- Tracking: Linear ENG-4878
- Target: before Phase 2 paging enablement

3) Telemetry ingestion latency monitoring
- Add panels for ingestion lag and a “data freshness” badge on canary dashboards.
- Evaluate shifting alert windows to depend on observed ingestion lag (or alert only when freshness is within bounds).
- Owner: Caleb Johnson + Logan Wright
- Tracking: new subtask under ENG-4877 / ENG-4878 (Talia to file)

Priority P1 (do alongside model coverage expansion)
4) Region/SKU-aware thresholds (manage complexity without exploding config)
- Keep default thresholds global per model, but allow overrides for known noisy regions/SKUs.
- Add config validation to prevent “override sprawl” (max overrides per model, require justification).
- Owner: Noah Patel + Vanessa Ortiz
- Tracking: ENG-4882

5) Expand prompt distribution coverage (v1)
- Add 1–2 additional workload profiles:
  - long-context prefill-heavy profile (tail-focused)
  - short prefill + longer decode profile
- Keep deterministic seeding so comparisons are stable across weeks.
- Owner: Rina Kobayashi
- Tracking: (Talia to file under ENG-4872)

6) Add KV cache hit-rate signal (evaluation)
- Decide if KV cache hit rate becomes a first-class canary metric.
- Concern: implementation complexity + increased noise if cache behavior differs between synthetic and real traffic.
- Output: short decision memo and either implement or explicitly defer.
- Owner: Sofia Ivanova + Omar El-Sayed
- Tracking: ENG-4875 follow-on

Priority P2 (required for rollout gates / “productization”)
7) Rollout gate integration policy
- Define exactly what “gate” means:
  - auto-pause expansion when paging signal fires for top models
  - require human ack for warnings
  - specify rollback criteria (duration + magnitude)
- Ensure change-management expectations align across Runtime/SRE/Releases/Product.
- Owner: Connor O’Brien + Marissa Cole + Paula Mendes
- Tracking: PM-642

8) Canary config change auditability
- Ensure model list and threshold changes are audited (who/when/why), and easy to diff.
- Owner: Quentin Harris + Logan Wright
- Tracking: control-plane config follow-up (Talia to file)

What we should keep doing
- Keep Phase 2 expansion incremental: add models first, then region; avoid simultaneous major runtime changes during threshold calibration.
- Continue weekly review of:
  - top 3 alerts (were they actionable?)
  - time-to-triage (what slowed us down?)
  - overhead metrics vs budget
- Treat on-call feedback as a primary input (if the runbook isn’t fast, the system fails even if it’s “correct”).

Open questions
- Do we want a single “perf regression score” per model that combines multiple signals, or keep separate alert streams per metric?
- Should baselines be computed from controlled load runs only (benchmark-lab), or can we safely incorporate canary observations when the system is stable?
- How far do we go on region-specific tuning before the config becomes unmanageable?

Appendix: notable incidents / threads
- False positive alert storm (root cause suspected: baseline drift + label/dedupe mismatch): Slack incidents/1770130402
- Sustained p95 regression page on top model (real issue): Slack incidents/1769034455

Notes to self (Noah)
- Don’t expand coverage until we’ve fixed dedupe + baseline drift. The cost of losing trust is higher than the cost of slower rollout.
- Keep the canary boring: predictable traffic, predictable labels, predictable alert behavior. Anything else becomes a second production system to operate.
